> 📍 **階層**: Home > Latest News > Deadline Nears For Education Department To Spend Special Ed Research Funds
For months, there have been concerns that the U.S. Department of Education could allow millions in special education research dollars to lapse. Now, a federal judge is stepping in.
U.S. District Judge Allison D. Burroughs is ordering the Education Department to update her by Monday about the status of the government’s education research funds.

As of last week, about $180 million in funding for the Education Department’s Institute of Education Sciences, or IES, which handles statistics, research and evaluation, remained unallocated and is set to expire at the end of September, Burroughs said. It’s unclear how much of that is intended for special education.
Advertisement - Continue Reading Below

The situation comes after a [report this spring](https://www.disabilityscoop.com/2026/04/27/ed-department-funding-for-special-education-research-may-soon-lapse/31970/) warned that just $11 million out of $77 million in the government’s budget for special education research and evaluation program had been spoken for. Subsequently, the National Center for Learning Disabilities, the Massachusetts Teachers Association and other stakeholders sued to prevent the funds from lapsing.
Burroughs said she opted to take a soft touch in the case based on assurances from the Education Department “that they intend to obligate the funds at issue before the deadline.”

However, she noted that “if it appears, as September 30 approaches, that defendants have misled the court and the funds will not be obligated by the deadline, the court may reconsider whether there has been undue delay warranting injunctive relief.”
Despite the agency’s assurances to the court, however, the status of the funding remains murky.

Meghan Burke, a professor of special education at Vanderbilt University, said that so far this year there have only been five awards from the National Center for Special Education Research, the special education funding arm of IES. All of the grants began this month. That volume is “lower than a typical year,” she said.

Jacqueline Rodriguez, CEO of the National Center for Learning Disabilities, which is part of the litigation, said she believes that it’s realistic for the funds to be released in light of the government’s assurances, but has limited information to go on.

“We don’t have a current number for exactly how much special education research funding remains unspent because the government has not publicly updated those figures,” Rodriguez said. But, she noted that requests for proposals have gone out, which she said was likely spurred by the lawsuit.
Preventing the funding from expiring, however, is critical, Rodriguez said.

“This funding supports research that gives us a much clearer picture of what students with disabilities are experiencing in schools and where they are not getting the support they need. It also supports work that benefits students in general education, as well as technical assistance that helps families understand and participate in the special education process,” she said. “If we don’t have that research and support, we’re making decisions without the information we need to know whether we’re actually serving students well.”

“IES intends to use its remaining FY25 funds to fully fund existing research grants, as well as to support other high-quality statistical and evaluation activities in service of its statutory obligations,” a department spokesperson said.

> 📍 **階層**: News > Poor sleep is driving conflict with managers, research finds
New research links poor sleep to heightened conflict with supervisors and higher-ranking colleagues, with implications for HR wellbeing strategies
Poor sleep causes conflict up the organisational ladder, and new research suggests HR leaders may have a direct role in addressing it.

The finding comes from a series of studies by the Johns Hopkins Carey Business School in Baltimore, Maryland. Collaborating teams at the University of South Carolina and the Walter Reed Army Institute of Research contributed to the work.

Employees who rest poorly are significantly more likely to clash with higher-ranking colleagues than with peers or subordinates. The research draws on data from US Army soldiers, tracing how fatigue shapes conflict across the organisational hierarchy.

The core finding: while poor rest raises the likelihood of friction generally, the sharpest escalation occurs upward. When rest was adequate, conflict remained low regardless of who was involved. When it deteriorated, arguments with supervisors increased far more than disputes between peers.
The full study, Sleep and Strife: The Effects of Sleep on Conflict within Organisational Hierarchy, was published in August 2026.
## **Why does poor sleep cause conflict with managers?**

Brian Gunia is a professor and area chair for management and organisation at the Johns Hopkins Carey Business School. He argues that self-control is the critical mechanism. Interacting with senior colleagues demands more behavioural regulation – suppressing frustration, choosing words with care, and staying within professional norms.

"Avoiding conflict with higher-rank individuals in organizations involves following strict workplace norms," said Gunia. "That requires more self-control, but we know that sleep problems compromise people's self-control."

Because the behavioural standards managing upward interactions are stricter, the impact of depleted self-control is most visible there. Peer-level interactions carry weaker social expectations, so the erosion is less pronounced.
"Employees starved for self-control simply find it harder to follow those workplace norms," Gunia added.
## **What can HR leaders do about poor sleep causing conflict?**

Interpersonal friction, the authors note, damages organisational performance by undermining collaboration – with flow-on effects for morale, productivity, and retention. In high-stakes environments such as healthcare, emergency services, and aviation, the risks are more acute. HR leaders managing teams in safety-critical roles may find that fatigue-related friction is already surfacing in performance data or interpersonal complaints.
"It seems critical for organizations to pull whatever levers they can to support employee sleep," the researchers conclude.

The research points to a specific intervention: sleep leadership. Gunia and colleagues have separately developed and studied this approach, in which managers and HR teams [actively encourage healthy rest among their employees.](https://www.hcamag.com/au/specialisation/mental-health/why-hr-should-encourage-employees-to-sleep-more/174576) Prior work shows it improves rest quality. Leaders trained in this way may also reduce the upward conflict that threatens team cohesion.
## **How should organisations act on the findings?**

Practical levers include reviewing scheduling and workload expectations, [establishing clearer norms around after-hours communication](https://www.hcamag.com/asia/specialisation/benefits/more-singapore-employers-have-after-hours-work-communication-policies/585288), and incorporating fatigue into employee wellbeing and mental health strategies. Gov. Maura Healey filed a $2.24 billion supplemental budget Wednesday that would pump more money into the workforce that supports SNAP benefit recipients and establish a new health care fund as the state prepares for federal funding cuts.

The state’s existing Health Safety Net Trust Fund, which covers the cost of care for uninsured and underinsured residents, is poised to see a ballooning deficit as residents lose their MassHealth coverage due to policy changes incorporated in the federal One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

The governor’s package calls for the creation of a Health Care Stabilization Fund, which Healey in her filing letter said would “support emerging health care needs, including new costs born from recent federal policy changes.”
“This fund will allow us to house surplus resources to support MassHealth, the Connector, and the Health Safety Net,” Healey wrote.

The bill envisions a funding mechanism for the health care account that diverts some excess capital gains that otherwise would go into the rainy day fund. Healey asked lawmakers to enact the bill “promptly” to close the fiscal 2026 books.

The state surtax on high earners has been consistently generating surplus funds that must be spent on education and transportation, according to a constitutional amendment approved in 2022. Non-surtax taxes have experienced less robust growth and fiscal experts over the years have warned against heavy spending of volatile capital gains revenues.

The governor’s bill would steer $41.5 million to the Department of Transitional Assistance, the agency that administers SNAP benefits and is also under acute strain due to the federal law. That amount includes $26.6 million to support DTA caseworkers, which Healey’s office said will enable Massachusetts to retain the 78 new employees hired this year and hire 10 more. It also encompasses about $15 million “to support technology improvements and additional staff support to improve payment accuracy and help the department meet new federal requirements,” Healey’s office said.
Massachusetts is at risk of losing substantial federal revenue if it fails to reduce its error rate for SNAP benefits.

Repurposing a pitch from her energy affordability bill, Healey is again proposing overhauling how utility companies purchase electricity for customers on basic service. As Healey faces a reelection challenge this November with affordability on the ballot, the maneuver is expected to save ratepayers $610 million.

Other policy highlights of the bill involve suspending the state’s gas tax for two months in response to higher prices stemming from the ongoing war in Iran and capping the resale price of concert tickets at 110 percent of the face value of the original ticket. As she detailed last week, Healey also wants to invest $2 million into a home visiting program for parents of newborns and $250,000 to the Massachusetts Child Psychiatry Access Program for Moms.
